title: {{NAME}} and the Last Watering Hole
moral: True courage means making the harder choice, even when no one is watching.

pages.content: The savanna stretched in every direction like a great golden ocean, and {{NAME}} stood at its edge feeling wonderfully, thrillingly small. He was the youngest wildlife guardian the Thornveld Reserve had ever appointed, a title that meant carrying a worn leather notebook, a pair of heavy binoculars, and more responsibility than most children his age could imagine. Acacia trees threw long purple shadows across the cracked earth, and somewhere in the shimmering distance a herd of elephants moved like slow grey clouds. {{NAME}} had been watching the watering hole for three days now. It was shrinking. Every morning the muddy ring around its edge grew wider, the water retreating a little further from the animals that desperately needed it. He pressed his binoculars to his eyes and wrote in his notebook: Day 3. Water level critical. Must decide by nightfall.

pages.content: The decision pressing on {{NAME}} was not a simple one. Two days' walk north, the river still ran full and cool, but to guide the animals there meant leading them across the territory of the Mwangi farming community, whose crops grew right up to the old migration path. Last season, a elephant herd had trampled through and destroyed an entire maize field. The farmers were angry and frightened, and {{NAME}} understood why. His friend and mentor, old Ranger Adaeze, had told him, 'The animals and the people both belong to this land. Your job is never to choose one over the other.' {{NAME}} sat on a warm rock and stared at his notebook until the words blurred. He could open the northern gate and hope for the best. He could wait and watch the watering hole shrink further. Or he could try the third option, the one that was far more difficult, the one no ranger before him had ever actually managed to pull off.

pages.content: {{NAME}} ran. He ran faster than he ever had, long dusty strides carrying him north along the fence line toward the Mwangi farmstead, his hat nearly flying off, his notebook bouncing against his hip. He had to reach Farmer Kofi before the elephants did. Kofi was a tall man with a serious face and hands rough as tree bark, and he met {{NAME}} at his gate with crossed arms and narrowed eyes. But {{NAME}} did not stop to catch his breath. He spread his notebook open on Kofi's fence post and showed him the maps, the water data, the migration lines, talking so fast his words tumbled over each other like a waterfall. He proposed a corridor, just a narrow strip of Kofi's eastern field, temporarily fenced with orange flags, wide enough for the animals to pass safely through without touching the crops. Kofi was silent for a very long time. Then, slowly, a smile moved across his weathered face. 'You came to ask,' Kofi said quietly. 'Not to take. That is different.'

pages.content: They worked through the golden hour together, {{NAME}} and Kofi, stringing bright orange flags along a winding path through the eastern edge of the farm. Ranger Adaeze arrived on her motorbike with additional flags and stood watching with an expression {{NAME}} had never seen on her face before. It looked almost like pride. As the last flag was tied, the ground began to vibrate, a deep thrumming that {{NAME}} felt in the soles of his boots. Then the elephants came, enormous and unhurried, their great grey heads swaying, their eyes ancient and calm. The lead matriarch paused at the entrance to the corridor and regarded {{NAME}} for a long, extraordinary moment, her dark eyes holding his. He did not move. He barely breathed. She stepped forward, and the whole herd followed, flowing through the orange-flagged path like a slow river, not a single flag disturbed, not a single crop touched. Kofi placed a hand on {{NAME}}'s shoulder, and neither of them said a word.

pages.content: Later, {{NAME}} sat on his favourite rock as the stars appeared one by one above the savanna, the air finally cool and fragrant with dry grass. He wrote in his notebook, but slowly now, savouring each word. The elephants had reached the river. Kofi had invited him to share a meal of maize and stew. Ranger Adaeze had said only three words as she rode away, but they were the best three words: 'Well done, Guardian.' {{NAME}} closed his notebook and leaned back, looking up at the enormous dark sky scattered with silver. His eyelids grew heavy, and the warm earth seemed to hold him gently, the way good places always do. The sounds of the savanna settled into a soft, steady lullaby around him, crickets and faraway frogs and the distant murmur of the herd. He was nearly asleep when he heard it: a sound he had never heard before, somewhere beyond the acacia grove, low and rhythmic and curious, as though the savanna itself was trying to tell him a secret.
